question: Menopause is a natural life stage affecting millions of women and has a major impact1 on their physical and mental health, working life2 and overall quality of life. In spite of this, menopause care is still not sufficiently integrated into the EU’s public health and employment policies3.

Between the Member States, there are significant discrepancies in early diagnosis, information, training of health professionals, access to appropriate health services and support for women in the workplace. Only some have developed national menopause policies, while others, such as Greece, do not have a framework on this particular matter.
In view of the need for a more systematic integration of the gender aspect into health and employment policies, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Does it plan to propose the development of a European strategy on menopause care?
What measures does it intend to take to help women in the workplace during premenopause, menopause and post-menopause, with a view to supporting them and preventing discrimination?

Does it intend to propose dedicated funding for research and innovation, the inclusion of menopause in EU public health programmes, combating menopause poverty, improving information and awareness and collecting comparable data on the impact of menopause on women’s health and employment and on health systems?

According to the European Institute of Women’s Health and surveys of post-menopausal women, up to 90 % reported having experienced symptoms at some point during the menopausal transition, with approximately half considering their symptoms bothersome (https://eurohealth.ie/wpcontent/uploads/2023/11/Menopause-Policy-Brief.pdf).

2 Menopausal women are the fastest growing group in the labour force, currently accounting for 11 % of the labour force in the G7 countries alone, a figure that is expected to increase in the coming years as the population ages (https://podcast.ilo.org/episode/is-the-menopause-a-workplace-issue).

3 The transition to menopause is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular, metabolic and neurological diseases, but EU prevention strategies rarely address these links in a systematic manner (see European Parliament 2025 Report on Gender Inequalities in Medical Research, Drug Development and Access to Care). 1
answer: EN E-003129/26 on behalf of the European Commission (28.10.2026) The EU Gender Equality Strategy1 recognises that women’s health experiences and conditions, including menopause, have not received sufficient attention in health research or treatment. It announces that the Commission will fund a study on the benefits of closing the women’s health gap related to certain conditions, including menopause.

EU occupational safety and health legislation, notably the EU Framework Directive 89/391/EEC2 provides that employers must assess and prevent all workplace health and safety risks, including those linked to menopause, also by considering the specificities of particularly sensitive risk groups.

This is supported, where relevant, by the Workplace Directive3 which sets workplace requirements such as temperature, ventilation and sanitary facilities. The Healthier Together initiative4 is the Commission’s policy framework for supporting Member States and stakeholders in health promotion and disease prevention, with a focus on vulnerable groups, including women and girls.

The Commission does not earmark specific funding for women’s health research under Horizon Europe5. The Health Cluster work programme6 offers funding opportunities for health research through competitive calls, which are broadly defined and open to innovative approaches addressing different thematic areas, including menopause and other women’s health conditions.

In the next Multiannual Financial Framework, the proposed European Competitiveness Fund7 has a strong focus on healthcare and health technologies. The support under its Health, Biotech, Agriculture and Bioeconomy window would allow to prioritise health promotion and disease prevention across the life course, including in the field of reproductive health.
1 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and

Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions, Gender Equality Strategy 2026-2030, COM(2026) 113 final. 2 Council Directive 89/391/EEC of 12 June 1989 on the introduction of measures to encourage improvements in the safety and health of workers at work, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=celex%3A31989L0391.

3 Council Directive 89/654/EEC of 30 November 1989 concerning the minimum safety and health requirements for the workplace, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:31989L0654. 4 https://health.ec.europa.eu/non-communicable-diseases/healthier-together-eu-non-communicable-diseasesinitiative_en. 5 https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.
